name: Shamrock Green
lede: Shamrock Green is a vivid green from Ridgway's 1912 plates that appears in just one of our 23,781 archive paintings, too saturated for most aged, varnished canvases.

sections.title: A vivid green, named for Ireland's emblem
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 plates give Shamrock Green at hue 33′′, tone i, on plate XXXII, and the Inter-Society Color Council's 1955 census files it, in block 131, as a vivid green, Munsell 3.0G 5.6/9.4 [1]. The same ISCC-NBS block also holds Irish-themed near-duplicates, *Blarney*, *Killarney*, and *Emerald Isle*, and Maerz and Paul date Killarney to 1912 [1].

Its nearest library neighbor is [[jade]], about 3.2 units away, with [[green]] close behind at 4.0 [1]. The name follows [[shamrock]], Ireland's three-leafed emblem, though none of our sources date the pairing itself, and the hex code alone cannot settle it [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this saturated green in a single one of 23,781 paintings, as photographed [2]. That one case, Félix Vallotton's 1917 *Church ruins in Hurlus*, a Swiss scene, uses it as a mid-tone, not a highlight or shadow [2]. A color this vivid rarely survives on an aged, varnished canvas, which is the likely reason for its near-absence rather than any rarity in nature [2]. The count is a computed color match, never a pigment identification [2].
